item.title: Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning.Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

item.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury.
item.description:
Neurology
Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. Among 105 patients (mean age 58 ± 19 years; 21% women; 53% Hispanic/Latino), the most common etiologies were intracerebral hemorrhage (45%), traumatic brain injury (43%), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (10%). Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy occurred in 31%. Semantic processing was detected in 13 patients (12%). Recovery of consciousness occurred in 77% of patients with semantic processing compared with 49% without semantic processing (odds ratio [OR] 3.5; 95% CI 0.9-13.5, p = 0.08). Functional recovery occurred in 42% with semantic processing compared with 14% without semantic processing (OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.2-16.6, p = 0.03). Semantic processing was highly specific but insensitive for predicting both recovery of consciousness (specificity 94%, sensitivity 18%) and functional recovery (specificity 92%, sensitivity 29%). After excluding patients who underwent withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy or died of non-neurologic medical complications, specificity increased to 100% for recovery of consciousness and 95% for functional recovery. EEG evidence of semantic processing can be detected in a subset of unresponsive patients with ABI during the acute phase of injury and is associated with favorable long-term outcomes. Semantic processing was a specific but insensitive biomarker of recovery, suggesting potential utility as a rule-in marker of preserved cognitive function. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: Posterior-lateral basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei hypoconnectivity in the inferior frontal cortex is associated with verbal fluency deficits in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia (Heidelberg, Germany)
Cognitive impairment is a core feature of schizophrenia and remains insufficiently addressed by current treatments. Increasing evidence implicates the cholinergic system, particularly the basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei (BFCN), in cognitive dysfunction. While structural alterations of the BFCN have been reported, alterations in their intrinsic functional connectivity (iFC) remain unclear. The present study examined the iFC of anterior and posterior BFCN subdivisions (aBFCN, pBFCN) in schizophrenia and tested associations with cognitive performance. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from the COBRE dataset were analyzed, including 73 healthy controls (HC) and 51 patients with schizophrenia (SCZ). Seed-based connectivity analyses were performed for aBFCN and pBFCN. Group differences were assessed voxel-wise, and group-dependent associations with phonemic verbal fluency (FAS) and processing speed (BACS-SC) were tested using hierarchical regression controlling for age, sex, IQ, and smoking status; verbal learning and memory (HVLT) was examined as a specificity analysis. Exploratory molecular mapping used normative PET-derived neurotransmitter maps, supplemented by spatial-autocorrelation-preserving null models. Distinct connectivity patterns of aBFCN and pBFCN were observed, consistent with previous reports in HC. Compared with HC, SCZ showed reduced pBFCN connectivity with a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis; BA44; p = 0.018, FWE-corrected), whereas no significant differences were observed for aBFCN. The Group × pBFCN-IFG connectivity interaction was significant for FAS (p = 0.014) but not BACS-SC (p = 0.762) or HVLT (p = 0.514). In SCZ, higher pBFCN-IFG connectivity was associated with better FAS performance. Descriptive molecular mapping showed above-average representation of M1 and α4β2 receptor maps as well as several non-cholinergic targets; however, no molecular target showed significant spatial correspondence after spatial-autocorrelation-aware testing and FDR correction. These findings provide evidence for selective pBFCN hypoconnectivity with the right inferior frontal gyrus in schizophrenia. Its association with verbal fluency suggests that disrupted pBFCN connectivity with the inferior frontal cortex may contribute to altered executive control processes involved in verbal fluency in schizophrenia. Together, these findings extend previous evidence of BFCN abnormalities in schizophrenia by demonstrating a systems-level functional alteration of pBFCN-cortical connectivity and its relationship with cognitive performance.

item.title: Decoupling language and emotion in the bilingual brain.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
In a recent article, Davydova et al. showed that affect labeling fails in a second, less-proficient language due to the amygdala-ventrolateral prefrontal cortex functional connectivity. This subcortical decoupling also explains the emotional blunting that bilinguals report when using their less-proficient language.

item.title: Orthographic repetition elicits enhancement without suppression at both the word- and character-levels in Chinese.
item.description:
International journal of psychophysiology : official journal of the International Organization of Psychophysiology
In Chinese, orthographic repetition (e.g., ""-"") modulates neural activity associated with orthographic processing around 200 ms after target onset, as indexed by the N200 enhancement effect. The present study combined time-frequency analysis with priming paradigms in two EEG experiments to determine whether orthographic repetition is accompanied by oscillatory power enhancement or suppression. In Experiment 1, complete repetition priming of two-character words elicited both a significant N200 enhancement effect and significant theta power enhancement relative to the control condition, whereas no significant N200 or theta-power enhancement was detected for semantic or phonological priming. To separate orthographic overlap from the concomitant phonological and semantic repetition inherent in complete repetition, Experiment 2 used partial orthographic repetition with single-character prime-target pairs that differed in phonology and semantics and replicated both effects. Exploratory participant-level correlations between the N200 and total theta effects were positive but nonsignificant in both experiments. A positive correlation between N200 enhancement and evoked theta enhancement reached the unadjusted significance threshold only in Experiment 2. These findings indicate that orthographic repetition is associated with enhancement rather than suppression of theta-band activity and that this pattern extends across word and character levels.

item.title: Altered pre-supplementary motor area recruitment during semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Inhibitory control dysfunction has been implicated in obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), but neuroimaging research has focused predominantly on motor response inhibition. Whether obsessive–compulsive traits are associated with altered neural recruitment during semantic inhibition remains unclear. Methods: Forty right-handed participants with lower or elevated obsessive–compulsive traits performed an fMRI adaptation of the Hayling Sentence Completion Task. Participants either selected an expected sentence completion (initiation) or suppressed this strongly prepotent response to select an unrelated word (inhibition). Whole-brain and anatomically defined region-of-interest (ROI) analyses examined task-related activation and Group × Condition interactions, with particular interest in the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and SMA proper. Results: Semantic inhibition produced a robust behavioural cost in reaction times and error rates, with no significant differences between groups. Whole-brain analysis identified the strongest inhibition-related activation in the left preSMA. The exploratory Group × Condition analysis also yielded its peak interaction in this region. Anatomically defined ROI analysis showed a significant Group × Condition interaction in the preSMA after family-wise error correction (t = 2.56, pFWE = .012), reflecting a larger inhibition-related increase in controls compared to individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits. The corresponding interaction in SMA proper did not reach statistical significance (t = 1.74, pFWE = .084). Conclusions: Elevated obsessive–compulsive traits were associated with altered preSMA recruitment during semantic inhibition in absence of behavioural impairment. This extends neural markers of obsessive–compulsive alterations from the domain of motor inhibition to that of semantic inhibition.

item.title: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Causally Supports the Memory Advantage of Reading Aloud
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Reading words aloud improves later recognition relative to reading them silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect. This advantage may reflect not only the distinctive sensorimotor information generated by production, but also cognitive control processes that prioritise this information during encoding. Given the central role of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in supporting cognitive control, we tested whether this region causally contributes to the production effect using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In a preregistered within-participant study, 40 adults completed three sessions in which TMS was delivered bilaterally to the DLPFC. They received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), expected to reduce DLPFC excitability; intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), expected to increase it; or sham stimulation. Participants then read words aloud or silently before completing an old/new recognition test with confidence and recollection judgements. There was a clear production effect: words read aloud were recognised more accurately and quickly, with greater confidence and more frequent recollection ratings, than words read silently. Crucially, cTBS reduced the accuracy advantage for aloud words relative to sham and iTBS. Exploratory receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) modeling approaches provided converging evidence that cTBS reduced the memory advantage for words read aloud. Stimulation did not reliably affect responses to new words. These findings provide the first causal evidence that the DLPFC helps make words read aloud more memorable, consistent with a role for cognitive control in prioritising the distinctive information generated by speaking.

item.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and language development: biological evidence from an integrative review.
item.description:
Developmental neurorehabilitation
Objective This study aimed to analyze scientific evidence on the relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and its potential implications for language development and speech fluency. Methods An integrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases between August 2025 and July 2026. The search strategy included terms related to vitamin B12, myelination, brain development, language, and speech. Original studies published in English investigating the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency on the central nervous system, neurodevelopment, or structural brain changes were included. Results Thirteen studies met the eligibility criteria and were synthesized through thematic narrative analysis. The findings indicated a relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and delayed neuropsychomotor development, impaired myelination, reduced white matter integrity, and structural brain abnormalities identified by neuroimaging. Furthermore, studies investigating the neural circuits underlying language showed that these same structures are essential for language organization and speech fluency, providing biological plausibility for a potential relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and impairments in these processes. Conclusion Vitamin B12 deficiency may adversely affect neurodevelopment and cerebral myelination, representing a potential mechanism underlying alterations in the maturation of neural circuits involved in language. These findings support the biological plausibility that vitamin B12 deficiency may contribute to impaired language development through disrupted cerebral myelination, although direct clinical evidence remains lacking.

item.title: Audio large language models align with human neural responses during spoken-language comprehension.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Audio large language models (audio LLMs) process continuous speech directly and transform it into progressively more abstract representations, providing a useful computational point of comparison with human spoken-language comprehension. Previous studies have reported model-brain correspondence for pretrained speech models and text-based language models, but it remains unclear which internal representations of audio LLMs are most closely associated with neural responses during online listening. We compared EEG responses from 41 native Mandarin listeners with internal representations from Qwen2-Audio, Qwen2.5-Omni, and Kimi-Audio in a Mandarin auditory semantic-violation paradigm that controlled sentence structure and event boundaries. We extracted speech-related and word-level semantic-update representations and quantified their incremental contributions to held-out EEG prediction beyond lower-level controls. Audio LLM representations improved EEG prediction beyond the acoustic envelope, phoneme onsets, and word onsets (Δr = 0.012, corrected P = 0.028). Prediction-score partitioning indicated that semantic violation primarily increased the overlap in EEG-predictive information between speech-related and semantic-update representations, rather than the unique contribution of either representation class. This pattern was relatively stable in Qwen2-Audio and Qwen2.5-Omni and directionally consistent, although statistically weaker, in Kimi-Audio. These findings provide component-level evidence that audio-conditioned model representations correspond to human neural responses during spoken-language comprehension, without implying mechanistic equivalence.

item.title: Differentiating language-specific from language-related network dynamics using dynamic functional connectivity analysis.
item.description:
Cognitive neurodynamics
UNLABELLED: Language processing is a highly complex dynamic neural activity that requires the recruitment of both regions critical for language processing and large-scale cognitive networks. Because language networks are interconnected and dynamically reconfigure their connections depending on task demand and complexity, it is challenging to differentiate language-specific networks form language-related cognitive networks during both resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) and task-based fMRI (tb-fMRI). Prior evidence demonstrated state-dependent differences in dynamic functional connectivity (FC) within identical networks across rest- and task-conditions. Based on this evidence, we hypothesized that examining dynamic FC patterns could help differentiate the functional specialization of large-scale neural networks in the human brain. Thus, we examined whether temporal patterns of dynamic FC could functionally differentiate networks engaged during a language task. Using a data-driven dynamic FC framework, we tested whether rest-task state transitions preferentially modulate subsets of large-scale networks. Specifically, we examined whether monotonic temporal trends in dynamic FC, used as a first-order approximation of sustained task engagement, were more prominent in networks showing task-sensitive dynamics, while others exhibited resting-state-like dynamics. We analyzed rs-fMRI and tb-fMRI data from 172 healthy participants (86 females, 27.6 ± 3.8 years old) from the Human Connectome Project. Dynamic FC analyses revealed significant state-dependent differences in correlation variability between rs-fMRI and tb-fMRI (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.001). A subset of networks exhibited task-sensitive temporal modulation, whereas other networks showed dynamic patterns closely paralleled resting-like dynamics without reaching statistical significance. These findings suggest that dynamic FC provides a useful framework for functionally distinguishing language-specific networks from language-related cognitive networks. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10579-0.

item.title: Aphasic status epilepticus presenting with prominent psychiatric symptoms: A case report.
item.description:
PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
Background Aphasic status epilepticus (ASE) is a subtype of nonconvulsive status epilepticus characterized by aphasia as its primary ictal manifestation. Although psychiatric symptoms are uncommon in ASE, they may obscure the diagnosis when present. We report an atypical case, presenting predominantly with agitation and irritability, which was rapidly diagnosed as ASE by electroencephalography (EEG) based on the abrupt symptom onset and neurological history. Case presentation A 49-year-old right-handed woman with alcohol use disorder was referred to our psychiatric hospital because of agitation, irritability, and disorganized thinking. Approximately 2 months before presentation to our hospital, she developed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 days after sustaining a head injury. A left posterior fossa subdural hematoma was diagnosed, and burr-hole evacuation was performed at a general hospital. She continued rehabilitation; however, 6 days before admission to our hospital, she suddenly developed incoherent speech with agitation and irritability, prompting referral to our psychiatric hospital. Neurological examination revealed sensory aphasia. Given the history of brain injury and abrupt symptom onset, EEG was performed and demonstrated left-dominant periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, confirming ASE. Antiseizure treatment resolved the EEG abnormalities and aphasia; however, aphasia, agitation, and irritability recurred with periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges. The symptoms improved with intravenous diazepam, and no recurrence was observed for >2 years following optimization of antiseizure medication. Conclusion ASE may present predominantly with psychiatric symptoms and be misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder. Recognizing symptom chronology and epileptogenic background is essential for prompting EEG evaluation and early diagnosis.
